title: Pipeline Architecture
summary: Identify the three major subsystems of a training pipeline architecture and explain the systems rationale for this decomposition.

blocks.md:
This lesson follows **Pipeline Architecture** in *Model Training* (Vol I). By the end you should be able to:

- Identify the three major subsystems of a training pipeline architecture and explain the systems rationale for this decomposition
- Apply the pipeline bottleneck model to identify the slowest comparable stage as the limit on end-to-end throughput
- Analyze why preprocessing latency can dominate input delivery even when the PCIe transfer itself is short
- Evaluate why changing batch size can alter optimization behavior even when hardware throughput improves
- Identify the systems mechanism (pinned memory) used for asynchronous host-to-device transfers

blocks.source: Vol I, Model Training, § Pipeline Architecture
blocks.md: A training step is not a single operation but a sequence of dependent stages: data must be loaded before computation can begin, forward passes must complete before backward passes start, and gradients must be computed before parameters can update. The speed of the slowest stage determines the speed of the entire system. Without pipelining, these stages serialize, idling the accelerator while the host prepares data or transfers batches across the bus.

blocks.title: Map of the section
blocks.md:
The section is organised as:

- Pipeline stages and accelerator bubbles
- Data pipeline
- Forward and backward pass
- Parameter updates
- Training state and checkpoints

Pay attention to: subsystem decomposition of training pipelines; pipeline bottleneck model and end-to-end throughput limits; CPU-side preprocessing and GIL bottlenecks; batch size scaling and learning rate interactions.

blocks.prompt: Think first: Explain why CPU-side tokenization and data augmentation can severely bottleneck GPU training even when the resulting tensor transfer across PCIe takes less than one millisecond.
blocks.md: A fast PCIe copy only shows that the transfer stage is short once a batch already exists; it says nothing about how long the CPU needed to create that batch. If CPU preprocessing takes 65 ms and GPU compute takes 80 ms, then with proper overlap the next batch can still be ready in time, but without overlap or with an unstable host service interval the GPU can see bubbles despite the sub-millisecond transfer. The practical consequence is that busy-time fractions alone are not peak arithmetic efficiency and do not prove a specific worker count; what matters is whether preprocessing can consistently supply the next batch before compute needs it.

questions.q: Which set of subsystems defines the chapter's high-level training system architecture, and what systems engineering advantage does this decomposition provide?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is B. The training architecture decomposes the system into three interconnected subsystems: the data pipeline (ingestion, transformation, batching), the training loop (forward pass, loss, backward pass, optimizer update), and the evaluation pipeline (validation metrics on held-out data). This separation enables engineers to diagnose bottlenecks by subsystem resource demands (host CPU/disk for data, accelerator compute/HBM for training loop, and periodic synchronization pauses for evaluation). The storage controller and compiler option describes compiler infrastructure rather than runtime training systems. The tokenizer and registry option describes MLOps lifecycle tools. The gradient aggregator option lists distributed implementation components rather than end-to-end training subsystems.
questions.hint: Think about: identify the three major subsystems of a training pipeline architecture and explain the systems rationale for this decomposition.
options: Storage controller, compiler intermediate representation, and runtime execution engine; this separates hardware target code generation from storage layout.

Data pipeline, training loop, and evaluation pipeline; this separates distinct resource profiles (CPU/storage I/O, accelerator compute/memory, and periodic validation) so bottlenecks can be isolated at subsystem interfaces.
Tokenizer, hyperparameter optimizer, and model registry; this organizes the model deployment lifecycle around developer interfaces.
Gradient aggregator, parameter server, and checkpoint restorer; this decomposes cloud service microservices.

questions.q: In a profiled training pipeline, CPU data preprocessing sustains \$4 GB/s on the same logical batch representation that host-to-device transfer and GPU consumption are being compared against. Host-to-device PCIe transfer sustains \$32 GB/s, and GPU compute consumes data at an equivalent rate of \$12 GB/s. Under the section's ideal-overlap pipeline model, what determines end-to-end throughput, and what is the best first engineering action?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is C. In the section's pipeline model, comparable stage rates are combined through a minimum: the slowest stage caps throughput even if transfer and compute are faster. Here preprocessing at \$4 GB/s is the limiting constraint, so the first goal is to raise input-side service rate and remove that bottleneck. An answer based on averaging ignores how pipelines work, and upgrading the PCIe or compute stage, neither of which limits throughput, does not change a system still waiting on preprocessing.
questions.hint: Think about: apply the pipeline bottleneck model to identify the slowest comparable stage as the limit on end-to-end throughput.
options: The average of the three rates, so the effective throughput is \$16 GB/s and all stages should be tuned evenly.
The PCIe transfer rate, because every batch must cross the bus before any compute can happen.
The minimum rate, \$4 GB/s from preprocessing, so the first action is to reduce the input-side bottleneck before tuning faster stages.
The GPU compute rate, because training pipelines are ultimately limited by accelerator execution speed rather than host stages.

questions.q: Scaling the training batch size by \$8× while keeping the learning rate and schedule unchanged guarantees the same model quality in less wall-clock time.
questions.explanation: False. A larger batch changes both the number of updates per epoch and the gradient statistics seen by the optimizer, so the old learning-rate schedule may no longer be appropriate. The section says validation is needed after a large batch-size change, and retuning may be needed rather than guaranteed.
questions.hint: Think about: evaluate why changing batch size can alter optimization behavior even when hardware throughput improves.

questions.q: In the chapter's staged system pipeline framework, what constitutes an "accelerator bubble" and what is the primary diagnostic step to resolve it?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is D. An accelerator bubble is defined as idle or underutilized accelerator time resulting from a throughput mismatch across the four pipeline stages (Data Loading & Preprocessing, Host-to-Device Transfer, Forward/Backward Compute, and Parameter Synchronization). Resolving bubbles requires profiling each stage to locate the limiting constraint and applying overlapping techniques such as asynchronous prefetching. The assertion of intentional synchronization misinterprets a performance inefficiency as a design feature. The SRAM cache eviction option confuses low-level cache misses with macro pipeline stalls. The ridge-point loss option misapplies roofline terminology to pipeline-level time allocation.
questions.hint: Think about: explain the systems definition of accelerator bubbles across the four pipeline stages and identify the diagnostic procedure to eliminate them.
options: An intentional synchronization barrier inserted by automatic differentiation to ensure memory coherence across gradient passes; resolved by disabling graph checks.
An on-chip SRAM cache eviction event caused by large transformer sequence lengths; resolved by switching to smaller embedding tables.
A loss of arithmetic intensity when batch sizes fall below the hardware ridge point; resolved by forcing FP64 accumulation.

Silicon idleness where accelerator ALUs wait for data loading, host-to-device PCIe transfer, or parameter synchronization; resolved by profiling the four pipeline stages to identify and overlap the slowest stage.

points: You can now identify the three major subsystems of a training pipeline architecture and explain the systems rationale for this decomposition.
You can now apply the pipeline bottleneck model to identify the slowest comparable stage as the limit on end-to-end throughput.
You can now analyze why preprocessing latency can dominate input delivery even when the PCIe transfer itself is short.
You can now evaluate why changing batch size can alter optimization behavior even when hardware throughput improves.
